content: Individuals diagnosed with diabetes should be provided with blood glucose monitoring (BGM) devices tailored to their specific circumstances, personal preferences, and treatment regimens. Patients who are on insulin therapy and using BGM should be encouraged to monitor their blood glucose levels at appropriate times based on their insulin regimen. This includes checking glucose levels during fasting, before meals and snacks, after meals, at bedtime, during the night, before, during, and after physical activity, when symptoms of hypoglycemia are present, after treating hypoglycemia until glucose levels return to normal, when hyperglycemia is suspected, and before and during critical activities such as driving. Healthcare professionals must recognize that not all blood glucose meters have the same level of accuracy. Only devices that have been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) or equivalent regulatory bodies in other regions should be used. These devices must be paired with unexpired test strips that are purchased from reputable pharmacies or licensed distributors and stored under appropriate conditions to maintain their reliability. Although the use of BGM in individuals who are not on insulin therapy has not consistently demonstrated significant reductions in A1C levels, it can still be beneficial in specific scenarios. For example, BGM may assist in making adjustments to meal plans, physical activity routines, or medications, particularly those that carry a risk of hypoglycemia, as part of a structured treatment adjustment program. Healthcare providers should also be aware of medications and other factors that may interfere with the accuracy of blood glucose meters.
